entities.summary:
Antiochus was a Seleucid prince and first-born child of the Seleucid monarchs Antiochus III the Great and Laodice III, inheriting the throne at a young age. His reign was marked by conflicts with neighboring kingdoms, particularly the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt, as well as internal power struggles within the Seleucid Empire.

Antiochus' most notable achievement was his attempt to spread Greek culture and religion throughout the eastern Mediterranean, which led to a significant clash with the Jewish community in Judea. His actions were seen as a threat by the Romans, who had long been wary of Seleucid expansionism.

The consequences of Antiochus' policies were far-reaching, leading to increased tensions between Jews and Greeks, and ultimately contributing to the Maccabean Revolt against the Seleucid Empire. The revolt, led by Mattathias and his sons, resulted in the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem and the establishment of a Jewish state.

Antiochus' legacy extends beyond his own reign, as he played a significant role in shaping the complex web of alliances and rivalries that characterized the ancient Mediterranean world. His actions also had a lasting impact on Jewish identity and culture, cementing the importance of religious freedom and autonomy.

The 192 BCE date etched into history marks not only the end of Antiochus' life but also the beginning of a new era in Jewish history, one marked by resistance against external forces and a renewed commitment to preserving Jewish traditions.

The significance of Antiochus lies not only in his own actions but also in the ripple effects they had on subsequent events and cultures. His reign serves as a pivotal moment in understanding the complex dynamics of ancient Mediterranean politics and the enduring importance of religious freedom and cultural identity.
